mcqs.q: Intraosseous anaesthesia involves depositing solution into the:
mcqs.explain: Intraosseous techniques (PDL, intraseptal, intraosseous) place LA into the cancellous bone adjacent to the tooth.

mcqs.q: The periodontal ligament (PDL) injection is primarily used as an:
opts: Alternative to the inferior alveolar nerve block
Way to anaesthetise the whole quadrant
mcqs.explain: The PDL (intraligamentary) injection is an alternative to the IANB, especially for one or two mandibular teeth.

mcqs.q: A key reason to choose a PDL injection in a child is that it:
opts: Avoids residual soft-tissue numbness and self-inflicted lip/tongue injury
Numbs both sides of the jaw
mcqs.explain: The PDL avoids lip/tongue numbness, reducing the risk of a child biting and injuring anaesthetised soft tissue.

mcqs.q: The PDL injection is a good option in a haemophiliac patient because it:
opts: Avoids a deep nerve block in highly vascular tissue
Replaces the need for clotting factors
mcqs.explain: When nerve blocks are contraindicated (e.g. haemophilia, anticoagulation), the localized PDL injection is a useful alternative.

mcqs.q: In a PDL injection, the anaesthetic reaches the apex by:
opts: Diffusing apically into the marrow/interseptal bone (not down the ligament)
Coursing directly down the periodontal ligament to the apex
mcqs.explain: Solution reaches the periapical tissues by diffusing apically into the marrow spaces and interseptal bone, not by flowing down the actual PDL.

mcqs.q: The recommended volume for a PDL injection is about:
mcqs.explain: Use only ~0.2 mL of solution over 20 seconds per root (each root of multi-rooted teeth).

mcqs.q: During a PDL injection, which finding indicates a successful technique?
opts: Significant resistance to injecting the solution
The solution flowing in with no resistance
mcqs.explain: Resistance to deposition is a good sign of success, indicating the solution is being forced into the dense PDL/bone.

mcqs.q: A PDL injection is contraindicated over a primary tooth with a permanent bud beneath because it may cause:
opts: Enamel hypoplasia of the developing permanent tooth
mcqs.explain: PDL injection above a primary tooth can cause enamel hypoplasia in the developing permanent successor; infiltration is preferred in primary teeth anyway.

mcqs.q: The intraseptal injection is mainly indicated for:
opts: Soft-tissue and bone anaesthesia during periodontal surgery
mcqs.explain: Its primary use is soft-tissue and bone anaesthesia for periodontal curettage and flap surgery; it gives poor/brief pulpal anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: A feature shared by the intraseptal and intraosseous injections is:
opts: Essentially zero chance of positive aspiration
mcqs.explain: Both deposit into bone with essentially zero aspiration risk and avoid lip/tongue numbness.

mcqs.q: In the intraseptal technique, the needle enters the interdental papilla at:
opts: 90° to the tissue, then advances 1–2 mm into the septum (0.2–0.4 mL)
Parallel to bone with no penetration
mcqs.explain: Enter the centre of the papilla at 90°, contact bone, push 1–2 mm into the interdental septum, and deposit 0.2–0.4 mL.

mcqs.q: Which are recognised intraosseous anaesthesia systems?
mcqs.explain: The three main intraosseous systems are Stabident, X-Tip and Intraflow.

mcqs.q: In the Stabident system, the perforator is:
opts: A solid 27-gauge wire on a slow-speed handpiece that drills the cortical plate
A hollow needle that injects directly
mcqs.explain: The perforator is a solid, beveled 27-gauge wire driven by a slow-speed handpiece to drill a hole through the cortical plate; LA is then injected through that hole.

mcqs.q: For intraosseous anaesthesia of one or two teeth, the volume injected into bone is about:
mcqs.explain: Inject 0.4–0.65 mL for one or two teeth (up to 1.8 mL when treating multiple teeth in a quadrant).

mcqs.q: The intraosseous perforation site is located:
opts: About 2 mm apical to the crossing of gingival-margin and interdental-papilla lines, distal to the tooth
At the apex of the tooth on the lingual side
In the floor of the mouth
mcqs.explain: Perforate 2 mm apical to where a horizontal (gingival margin) line meets a vertical (interdental papilla) line, on the distal of the tooth to be treated.

mcqs.q: The intrapulpal injection is used:
opts: When all other techniques have failed, or as an endodontic adjunct
mcqs.explain: Intrapulpal injection is a last resort when other methods fail or as an adjunct during endodontic therapy, most often on mandibular molars.

mcqs.q: Which is characteristic of the intrapulpal injection?
opts: Intense, instantaneous pain that passes quickly, with profound anaesthesia in ~30 s
mcqs.explain: It usually causes brief, intense pain on injection but then provides profound, immediate anaesthesia (within ~30 s); aspiration risk is zero.

mcqs.q: The volume deposited in an intrapulpal injection is about:
opts: 0.2–0.3 mL under pressure into the pulp chamber
mcqs.explain: Place the needle firmly into the pulp chamber and deposit about 0.2–0.3 mL under mild/moderate pressure.

mcqs.q: Bending the needle is acceptable in which injections?
mcqs.explain: Bending is acceptable only for the PDL and intrapulpal injections (a separated needle is easily retrieved); all other injections must be given without bending.

mcqs.q: An advantage of the PDL over the IANB for treating teeth in both mandibular quadrants is that it:
opts: Avoids a bilateral inferior alveolar nerve block
mcqs.explain: Using PDL injections lets you treat isolated teeth in both quadrants in one visit while avoiding a bilateral IANB (and its bilateral soft-tissue numbness).

mcqs.q: A recognised disadvantage of the PDL injection is:
opts: Post-injection discomfort that may last 2–3 days
mcqs.explain: Disadvantages include leakage with a nasty taste, difficult distal access on some molars, the need for a strong/special syringe, possible focal tissue damage, and post-injection soreness for 2–3 days.

mcqs.q: Why is the intraseptal injection unsuitable for an extraction?
opts: It provides only poor, brief pulpal anaesthesia
It has a high aspiration risk
mcqs.explain: The intraseptal injection gives only poor/brief pulpal anaesthesia, so it is not recommended for extractions or restorative work.

mcqs.q: With lidocaine + 1:100,000 epinephrine, the PDL injection provides pulpal anaesthesia lasting roughly:
mcqs.explain: A PDL injection of lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine gives pulpal anaesthesia of about 5 to 55 minutes' duration.

mcqs.q: During the intraosseous technique, the slow-speed handpiece is used to penetrate bone with a:
opts: Pecking motion until resistance is lost
mcqs.explain: Hold the perforator perpendicular to the cortex and activate the slow-speed handpiece with a pecking motion until resistance is lost (the bur breaks through).

saqs.a: PDL (periodontal ligament/intraligamentary), intraseptal, intraosseous, and intrapulpal injections — all deposit into bone/pulp when conventional blocks fail or are unsuitable.

saqs.q: Give the indications for a PDL injection.
saqs.a: One/two mandibular teeth in a quadrant; isolated teeth in both quadrants (avoid bilateral IANB); children (no residual soft-tissue numbness); when blocks are contraindicated (haemophilia); and to help localise/diagnose mandibular pain.

saqs.q: Explain how a PDL injection works and one sign of success.
saqs.a: The solution diffuses apically into the marrow/interseptal bone (not down the ligament) to reach the periapical tissues. Resistance to injection is a good sign of success.

saqs.q: Describe the intraseptal injection technique and use.
saqs.a: For periodontal surgery (soft tissue + bone). 27G needle into the centre of the interdental papilla at 90°, contact bone, advance 1–2 mm into the septum, deposit 0.2–0.4 mL. Poor pulpal anaesthesia; zero aspiration.

A perforator (solid 27G wire on a slow handpiece) drills the cortical plate distal to the tooth (2 mm apical to the gingival-margin/papilla crossing); a 27G needle then injects 0.4–0.65 mL into the cancellous bone. Zero aspiration; no lip/tongue numbness.

A last resort (or endodontic adjunct), usually on mandibular molars: needle placed firmly into the pulp chamber, 0.2–0.3 mL under pressure. Causes brief intense pain then profound immediate anaesthesia; zero aspiration.

saqs.q: In which injections is bending the needle acceptable, and why?
saqs.a: Only the PDL and intrapulpal injections, because a separated needle can be easily retrieved. All other injections must be given without bending the needle.
